newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Albania moves to smother violent unrest.
newsitem.headline: Albania moves to smother violent unrest.

text.p: Albania's beleaguered government moved to smother the violent unrest sweeping the impoverished Balkan state as one of its diplomats acknowledged that part of the south was out of control.

After weeks of unrest sparked by the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes, officials issued orders to shoot armed rioters on sight, imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew and curbed press freedoms after parliament declared a state of emergency.
Tanks were spotted in the southern town of Gjirokaster and gunfire from automatic weapons was occasionally heard there on Monday, Greek diplomats and eyewitnesses said.

"At least five or six tanks are inside the town now and have taken up key positions. There has been sporadic gunfire from automatic weapons throughout the day," said a Greek consulate official in Gjirokaster who was contacted by Reuters from Greece by telephone and requested anonymity.
An Albanian army source in Tirana said there were tanks near Gjirokaster but did not confirm that any were in the town itself.
"There are tanks near the town. They are not undertaking any offensive operations. They moved a bit out of the garrison near Gjirokaster," the source said.

In the southern port town of Vlore, set ablaze and plundered by armed mobs of Albanians enraged by the loss of their savings, 35 foreigners were plucked to safety by giant Chinook helicopters sent by Italy and flown to the Italian port of Brindisi.
The Italian Foreign Ministry said they included 20 Italians, four Germans, one Dutch citizen and at least three Greek nationals. Ten of them were reporters.
At least 12 people were reported killed at the weekend after crowds in several southern towns raided weapons depots and went on a rampage of burning and looting.
The United States said on Monday it strongly regretted Albania's imposition of emergency measures and a vote by the country's parliament to re-elect President Sali Berisha.

"We strongly regret the measures taken by the parliament and government today to, in effect, introduce a state of emergency and to introduce censorship of the Albanian press," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"We're very concerned that the state of emergency declared by the parliament today is being used to stifle legitimate free expression."
Russia said it was deeply concerned by events in Albania, Interfax news agency reported.
Italy is calling for a European Union meeting on Albania and Prime Minister Romano Prodi told Berisha in a telephone conversation on Monday that he hoped a political solution could be found.
International institutions should organise financial aid for Albania, Rome authorities said.
Italy fears a continuing crisis in the small Balkan country could lead to a new mass exodus of Albanians across the Adriatic.

The Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly urged an immediate end to the violence and Europe's top security body, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said it too was closely monitoring the situation.
Part of southern Albania is out of the control of the authorities, the country's ambassador to Britain Pavli Mihal Qesku said on Monday.

"It seems that Vlore is out of control and so is Sarande and a stretch of land along the coast," Qesku said on Britain's Channel Four television news. "But that is only a fraction of the country. In the rest of the country the government has control of everything," he said.
Qesku said measures being taken were not aimed at ordinary Albanians.
"It is not the people who will be shot," he said. "It is only the bands of terrorists, only the hard core of terrorists who will be shot if they don't hand in their weapons."
Qesku defended the government's handling of the crisis, saying it had prepared a package to resolve the economic crisis but the opposition had refused to listen.
In the capital Tirana, parliament elected Berisha to a second five-year term on Monday after voting unanimously on Sunday to declare an emergency.
The deputies issued a deadline of 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Monday for "armed rebels" to surrender their weapons or security forces would shoot them without warning.

Albanian state television said police had been given powers to shoot stone-throwers on sight and arrest anyone not in possession of valid identity papers in the mainly Moslem nation. A curfew would be in force between 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) and 7 a.m. (0600 GMT).
In Vienna, a spokesman for Berisha dismissed the unrest as the work of criminals intent on toppling the government.

"This is a rebellion of ordinary and political criminals who are trying to topple the legitimate power," Genc Pollo, a member of parliament for the ruling Democratic Party and Berisha's spokesman, told Austrian state radio.
Berisha himself blamed "communist rebels helped and financed by foreign espionage services" for the violence and vowed to use the "iron hand" of the law to quash the uprising.
In Athens, Deputy Foreign Minister Yiannos Kranidiotis said the Greek army was watching the border with Albania closely in case of a mass exodus of people fleeing the violence.
